description: Your database doesn't just store data — it can run code. Why logic lives next to your rows, and the building blocks: procedures, functions, sequences, and metadata.

screens.body: You've been treating your database like a filing cabinet: put data in, take data out. But databases like Oracle and Postgres can also RUN code — right there, next to the data. That's database programming, and it's the whole subject of CPRG 307.

options: Run code next to the data, not just store it
Store files and images
Replace your backend completely
check.question: Database programming means your database can…

screens.heading: Your database can think
screens.keyPoint: A database can run logic, not just store rows.

screens.body: Why bother? Two reasons. First, speed: logic running inside the database doesn't wait on network trips back and forth to your app. Second, safety: a rule enforced in the database applies no matter which app, script, or person touches the data. Nobody can sneak around it.

options: No network round-trips, and rules nothing can bypass
It makes the database look cooler
It deletes the need for backups
check.question: Logic in the database wins because…

screens.heading: Why code belongs next to data
screens.keyPoint: Faster (no round-trips) and safer (no bypassing the rules).

screens.body: Database logic comes in named, reusable chunks called executable units. A procedure DOES something (update all prices). A function COMPUTES something and hands you back a value (what's this order's total?). A package BUNDLES related procedures and functions together, like a folder for code. Grouping related logic means you write it once and call it from anywhere.

options: A table with extra columns
A single SQL query
A named, reusable chunk of database logic
check.question: An executable unit is…

screens.heading: Executable units
screens.keyPoint: Procedures do, functions compute, packages bundle.

screens.body: Not all database logic sticks around. An anonymous block is a one-off: you write it, run it, it's gone — great for quick admin tasks. A stored procedure or function is resident: it LIVES in the database, has a name, and anyone with permission can call it tomorrow. Temporary for experiments, resident for the real thing.

options: An anonymous block runs once and disappears
A stored procedure runs once and disappears
They are exactly the same thing
check.question: Temporary vs resident logic:

screens.heading: Temporary vs resident
screens.keyPoint: Anonymous blocks are one-offs; stored units live in the DB.

screens.body: Here's the key mental model: when database logic runs, it reaches straight into the stored data — reads rows, changes rows, all in one execution. A funds-transfer procedure doesn't ask your app for the balances; it reads both accounts, subtracts from one, adds to the other, and it's done. Logic + data, one trip, no middleman.

options: It reads and writes rows directly during execution
It emails the rows to your app first
It only works on one row at a time
check.question: How does database logic interact with stored data?

screens.heading: Logic with its hands on the data
screens.keyPoint: Database logic reads and writes rows directly — no middleman.

screens.body: Ever wonder where order numbers come from? A sequence is a database-managed number machine: every time you ask, it hands you the next unique value — 1001, 1002, 1003 — even if a hundred users ask at once. Nobody gets a duplicate, and your app code never has to coordinate. That's the pattern: the database supplies ordered, unique values independently of application logic.

options: A list of table names
A kind of backup
A database-managed machine handing out unique numbers
check.question: A sequence is…

code.snippet:
CREATE SEQUENCE order_seq START WITH 1001;

-- every call hands out the next number, safely
SELECT order_seq.NEXTVAL FROM dual; -- 1001
SELECT order_seq.NEXTVAL FROM dual; -- 1002

screens.heading: Sequences: the number machine
screens.keyPoint: Sequences hand out unique, ordered numbers — no duplicates, ever.

screens.body: Plot twist: the database keeps data ABOUT itself. Which tables exist? What columns does the orders table have? That info lives in the data dictionary — metadata tables you can query like any other data. Your app can literally ask the database to describe its own structure. Handy when you're writing tools, migrations, or just exploring a database you inherited.

options: Data about the database's own structure
Deleted rows waiting to be restored
The database's error logs
check.question: Metadata (the data dictionary) is…

screens.heading: Metadata: the database knows itself
screens.keyPoint: The data dictionary describes the DB's own structure — and you can query it.

title: Why Put Code in the Database?
